ABOUT

Jay Pimple

architecture student

While pursuing my bachelors in architecture at Kamla Raheja Vidyanidhi Institute for Architecture and Environmental Studies, the studios developed my understanding and philosophy about architecture and design.

While designing the academic projects, I developed an understanding that architecture, not always symbolic, is always interacting with people through spaces and programmes, shaping experiences and functionality. Design of such architecture should be RESPONSIVE, that is, responsive to the site, the context, the demands that the existing have and the demands of those that will inhabit it.

I have consistently explored form, space and attempted to reimagine systems, programmes, their roles in society and how architecture can help shape and redefine them. I am committed to exploring and expanding my knowledge, allowing me to engage in the larger responsibility that architecture has towards society.

01

SYMBIOTIC HOUSING

SEMESTER VII

The studio aimed to explore a means to formalise rental housing within the city, to bridge the gap between the growing demand of housing for bachelors and the shortfall of supply. It proposes a symbiotic system of plugins on cessed building sites that reimagine the built form of the SRA tenements while providing space for a rental component. The design explores how terraces and voids respond to constricting cessed sites to achieve proper light, ventilation and quality of life.

02

PROJECT RELEASE

SEMESTER VI

The project redesigns the Horticulture Department at Ooty, Tamil Nadu. The design generates a vertical stack of programmes to RELEASE the surrounding ground of built form, freeing it for experiments and plantations. The lower floors house the public programmes: a double-heighted farmer’s market, cafeteria and a public library. The upper floors stack the offices of the Horticulture Department, with intermediate inserts of double-heighted open spaces accessible to the public. The roof houses an amphitheatre allowing the public to access the very top of the structure, diminishing its domineering outlook and giving it to the people.

03

HOLYSTIC INFORMALITIES

SEMESTER VII

The exercise documented the Babulnath Temple at Malabar Hill and its role as a datum that influences the morphology of the settlements and the informality, through its programme that performs as a magnet for vendors and devotees. The panel is a plan of the precinct marking the strings of informality along its entrance, the foothill of the climb and the ascent to the mandir, with blow-ups of activities and informalities associated with the precinct.

05

SCHOOLING LIBRARIES

SEMESTER VI

Set inside the density of Kalbadevi, the school reimagines the interaction of institutions with the public. It houses ancillary public programmes, such as an auditorium, a stationery shop and a medical clinic, that can function simultaneously as the school hours go on. The library of the school opens itself up to the public, harnessing the temporality of its space and expanding. The school pushes the built form to the periphery of the plot to enable an open, playable ground for the children, despite the small size of the plot. Spaces on every floor terrace themselves to form places for hanging out and sitting, overlooking the playground.

06

THE BOULEUTERION

SEMESTER IV

Situated on the hill of the Junagadh Fort, the building places itself along an existing road that winds up the hill. It reimagines the ideas behind archetypal parliament houses, which have a look of authority and broadness in the facade, by making it sinuous and accessible to the public. The programmes are housed in horizontal pockets along the path that look out onto the valley, harnessing its beauty through strategic viewpoints. The main hall of the bouleuterion uses the shape of a circle to maintain a certain democracy, where people can come and access meetings. Other programmes include offices, restaurants, bike stations and archival rooms accessible to the public.

07

PROJECT X - FOLIES

SEMESTER III

The project sits on the grid of the salt pans at Wadala, plugging in folies at nodes that house programmes responding to the requirements around them. The folies have a mix of programmes catering to the public as well as the workers who inhabit the site daily. The programmes include resting spaces, washrooms, public markets, cold storages, salt storages and an extension of fishing piers that activate during the season when the water levels rise and contain fish, improving the current infrastructure for pisciculture.

08

STRUCTURING SKYSCRAPERS

SEMESTER VII

The studio focused on understanding the structural systems involved in high-rise buildings that are designed to withstand earthquakes, wind loads, lateral loads and torsion. The model is a study of the HSBC Tower by Norman Foster, located in Hong Kong. It examines the systems of load transfer through suspended trusses held by two main structural cores. The model was tested on an earthquake simulator.

DOCUMENTINGJUNAGADH

STUDY
TRIP
PANEL

SEMESTER IV

The documentation exercise took place in Junagadh, Gujarat. The region had versatile rulers who influenced its architectural language. The monuments, constructed to uphold a certain legacy, carry influences of Gothic architecture, Islamic architecture and the Indian architecture of the region.

The structures in the panel are the Mohabbat Maqbara and Bahauddin Maqbara, both constructed as tombs for the rulers. The panel documents the architectural language, the collage of European, Islamic and Indian elements, and the structural system of these load-bearing buildings that uphold the heavy solid dome.
